blocks.text: Propositional equivalence explains when two logical expressions have the same meaning. Expressions that look different may give the same result. Equivalence is checked with truth tables: if two expressions have the same truth value in every case, they are equivalent. The symbol ≡ is used to show equivalence.
Example: exclusive OR written two ways

Expression 1, (A AND NOT B) OR (B AND NOT A), is equivalent to Expression 2, (A OR B) AND (NOT A OR NOT B). Both are true exactly when one of A and B is true but not both, which is called exclusive OR (XOR) (Fig 2.6).

blocks.alt: A box stating that two propositional expressions are logically equivalent: Expression 1, (A AND NOT B) OR (B AND NOT A), and Expression 2, (A OR B) AND (NOT A OR NOT B), joined by a double arrow; both are true in the same cases (XOR). A Venn diagram shades A only and B only, leaving the overlap and the outside unshaded, with a four-part key. A truth table and a closing line Therefore: Expression 1 is equivalent to Expression 2.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.6: Two logically equivalent propositional expressions, by Venn diagram and truth table (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.6).
blocks.long_description: Key: A AND NOT B; B AND NOT A; Neither A nor B; A AND B (not included). Truth table rows (A, B, Expression 1, Expression 2): F F F F; F T T T; T F T T; T T F F.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Equivalent expressions may look different but always give the same result; they help simplify complex logic.

Equivalent expressions are identified with truth tables: each expression is tested for all possible truth values, and if the results match in every case they are equivalent. Logical laws also help identify equivalence and simplify expressions.

Equivalence lets us replace a complex expression with a simpler one, saving time and effort. In programming, simpler equivalent conditions make code more efficient and help avoid logical errors, and they keep reasoning and decisions correct.
